 Toledo budget deadline looms after income tax defeat 
 The budget is due to city council members Sunday, so will layoffs make it into the final version? By Shaun Hegarty Published : Nov. 9, 2026 at 7:50 PM EST | Updated : 1 hour ago Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - We’re just a few days away from the deadline for the Toledo city budget to be finished. Some hard choices need to be made. 
 Voters said “no” to an income tax increase, which could mean layoffs as we get into 2027. The mayor and his staff said that if the income tax measure didn’t pass, that layoffs were on the radar. The budget is due to city council members Sunday, so will layoffs make it into the final version?
 It might be too early to think about swimming but in the last few weeks, swimming pool were mentioned as a possible budget casualty if Toledo’s quarter percent income tax failed. It has now failed at the ballot box, so what comes next? 
 “Clearly the administration is going to have to have major proposals for reductions in expenditures. And that’s what we’re going to be waiting on to see what they do,” said Toledo city councilman George Sarantou (I). 
 Councilman Sarantou is one of the council members waiting for that budget, and maybe more importantly the cuts that are planned. He does not want to see police or fire layoffs but they have been discussed. 
 “We have to see what they present to us and we’ll have to determine as a council what are the priorities. In my book, public safety is number one. That’s our biggest and huge responsibility that we have and we have to preserve public safety as much as possible,” said Sarantou. 
 So what gets cut? A city spokeswoman told us Monday that they are still finalizing budget decisions. Then council members get to dissect them. 
 “We have to see what those numbers are specifically and what the negative effect is. You certainly cannot decimate a department or several departments in the city of Toledo. All of the departments have to be functioning, not only because of federal and state funding but because we have to serve the public,” said Sarantou.
